messages.subject: Sooty shearwaters and the weather
messages.body_plain:
This is not a distance sampling problem, but I would be very
interested in comments from statistically minded ornithologists or
biologists on possible explanations.

Regular surveys of birds found dead on New Zealand beaches have
been carried out by Ornithological Society members since the 60's
and summaries by month are published annually in the journal
Notornis.

I'm not even sure what these finds are likely to indicate as far as
population numbers are concerned.  Do high levels of dead birds
show large populations at sea (a good thing) or large losses at sea
(a bad thing).

My main interest was to see what patterns there were in the sooty
shearwater figures, so I took the monthly figures (birds found per
km) for this species over the last 34 years or so.  A log
transformation gave an approximately normal distribution.  After the
monthly pattern had been removed, I looked at the 34 yearly base
rates to see if there were any year to year patterns to be seen.
The first surprise was that the figures recovered in any particular
year were uncorrelated with those found in the previous year, or the
year before that, but there was a significant correlation with the
numbers found three years previously.  (r = 0.50 p = 0.005.)

Any suggestions?  My first thought was that possibly the birds
spent their first three years away at sea and didn't return to their
New Zealand breeding grounds for that time so a large number of
fledglings this year will be reflected three years later.  However, I
can't find any mention of this anywhere.

My next thought was that the three year correlation may be
connected with a three year pattern in the weather, so I tried
correlating the bird data with the average NZ temperature and
pressure and the Southern Oscillation Index over the same period.
Temperature and SOI produced no significant correlations but the
local pressure did.  Bird numbers correlated well (r = -0.36 p =
0.05) with the local pressure two years previously but even more
strongly with the pressure the year after the birds were found! (r = -
0.44  p = 0.01)  I guess atmospheric pressure measures weather in
a general way but can bird deaths one year be used to predict the
weather a year later?  Oddly enough, correlations within the
pressure series showed nothing at three years.  There was a
possible auto-correlation at two years (r = -0.3 p = 0.1) but that
was about it.

How can we reconcile a three year correlation between bird
numbers with a sort of three year connection (+1 and -2) with
weather when there is no three year connection within the weather
itself?

Any ideas appreciated - I'm at a loss.

Derek

Derek Christie
Science Department
The Waikato Polytechnic
Hamilton
New Zealand

messages.subject: Info, DISTANCE questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear DISTANCE listserver,
I am new to the game; I have the following questions and would appreciate
your feedback and thoughts:

1. Has anybody used DISTANCE sampling for land-based coastal surveys ?
And how does one address the issue of random transect/point locations ?

2. I have old transect data which were collected with radial distances (not
perpendicular),
and I like to get density estimates from that; references or help on how to
analyze these data would be appreciated.
Would there be any chance to use current DISTANCE software for that ?

3. I am always grateful for arguments and ways to better convince
people/agencies using
DISTANCE sampling + software (instead of e.g. relative abundance and
indexes) ...

Thanks in advance and best regards

 Falk

PS. I will be going in the field whole May, but would be happy to post a
summary of
replies, if requested.

messages.subject: Some question
messages.body_plain:
Dear DISTANCE listserver,

I have the following questions and would appreciate your help.

I collected certain data of sika deer using night spotlight counts every
day along a fixed route in an area. These data include perpendicular
distance and cluster size of sika deer. I calculated deer density of the
area using Distance 2.2 (Distance for Win can not work under Japanese
Windows OS), and now I want to compare deer densities between two
periods. I tried to compare densities using the 95% confidence
intervals, but I found the 95% confidence intervals given by Distance
2.2 are not symmetric. Should someone tall me how I should statistically
compare two density estimate results from distance sampling method?

Sincerely,
Yuchun Li

messages.subject: Re: Some question
messages.body_plain:
> > I collected certain data of sika deer using night spotlight counts every
> > day along a fixed route in an area. These data include perpendicular
> > distance and cluster size of sika deer. I calculated deer density of the
> > area using Distance 2.2 (Distance for Win can not work under Japanese
> > Windows OS), and now I want to compare deer densities between two
> > periods. I tried to compare densities using the 95% confidence
> > intervals, but I found the 95% confidence intervals given by Distance
> > 2.2 are not symmetric. Should someone tall me how I should statistically
> > compare two density estimate results from distance sampling method?

Assessing differences from whether confidence intervals overlap is not
valid whether or not they are symmetric.  An approximate z-test is
obtained by taking the statistic

                   D^_1 - D^_2
  z  =  -----------------------------------
        sqrt[{se(D^_1)}**2 + {se(D^_2)}**2]

See p381 of the Distance Sampling book for similar tests.  (The book is
available from RUWPA's web pages if you don't have a copy - see below.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: line transect width
messages.body_plain:
I'm embarking on a survey of Black-capped Vireos in Northern Mexico.  I have
decided to use Line Transect methodology and analyze the data using the
latest downloadable version of Distance.  I will be using lines with
distance intervals, probably three (0-20, 20-60, 60-120 m; letting 120 m =
w) on each side of the line.  I assume the shape of the line transect,
complete with intervals, is a rectangle.  If this is true then birds singing
adjacent to, but not on, either end of the center line of a line transect
are not to be counted.  Is this true?  If so, how are these birds accounted
for?  Are they just ignored?  While I can understand not counting birds
beyond the outermost limit of the sampling intervals, perpendicular to the
center line (> w), due to problems with assigning it to a distance interval,
it would be very frustrating to hear a bird sing just adjacent to either end
of the center line and not be able to count it.  Can anyone help me out on
this?

Craig Farquhar, Ph.D.
Wildife Diversity Program
Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
3000 S IH-35, Ste. 100
Austin, Texas  78704

off: 512-912-7018
fax: 512-912-7058

messages.subject: Re: poststratification
messages.body_plain:
> > a) poststratification is an ad hoc method which can yield too small
> > variances if it is done after having seen the data.. Is it also true if we
> > use an "objective" classification of the habitat type based on most
> > important vegetal associations of study area?

Post-stratification is not ad hoc if it is based on an objective
covariate.  It is if it is based on the response - and that can lead to
serious underestimation of variance.  Your procedure should be fine.  We
also use it for deer (dung) surveys.

> > b) if visibility changes as a function of habitat I'd use habitat-sp銃cific
> > detection functions. I used a pooled estimate as more robust due to a
> > limited sample size

That is OK, provided you don't quote density or abundance estimates by
habitat type.  In other words, pooling robustness ensures you get a good
estimate of total abundance (if the main assumptions hold), but you get
biased estimates of abundance by habitat.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: poststratification
messages.body_plain:
Dear DISTANCE users,

I have the following question and would appreciate your opinion.

I've collected line transect data on roe and fallow deer. Transects were
randomly distributed on the study area. In data analysis I found that
postratification of samples following the more important habitat types
(such as evergreen, decidous woods, open areas ...) reduced the variance of
the density estimates. Such poststratification was also based on objective
measurements of habitat "visibility" showing that it decreased from open
area to evergreen woods.

I received two negative comments about this procedure:

a) poststratification is an ad hoc method which can yield too small
variances if it is done after having seen the data.. Is it also true if we
use an "objective" classification of the habitat type based on most
important vegetal associations of study area?

b) if visibility changes as a function of habitat I'd use habitat-sp銃cific
detection functions. I used a pooled estimate as more robust due to a
limited sample size

thank you in advance,

                            Stefano Focardi
